title: The Evening Brief: ETF inflows hold, but late-week selling tests rebound narrative
dek: Bitcoin ETFs logged their third consecutive weekly inflow on July 24, but sharp late-week outflows and a critical institutional divide on stablecoin regulation signal persistent uncertainty ahead of the FOMC decision.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: The desk's market boards and the ETF reporting both show strain: three weeks of inflows mask $465 million in Thursday-Friday outflows, while major Wall Street firms publicly split on the Clarity Act's core terms just before the Senate's August 8 recess deadline.
bottom_line: Bitcoin ETFs posted their third consecutive weekly inflow, but late-week selling totaling $465 million suggests institutional conviction remains tentative, and the desk's boards show major assets deep underwater from 12-month highs. Whale transfers ran onto exchanges over the prior 24 hours. Regulatory progress on the Clarity Act accelerated with five major Wall Street firms endorsing the bill ahead of the Senate's August 8 recess, yet the endorsements masked a JPMorgan split with the crypto industry on stablecoin yield terms. Operational shifts accelerated: Lido reshaped Ethereum staking with mandatory operator bonds, Circle became the largest U.S. blockchain patent holder, Core Scientific pivoted decisively to AI infrastructure, POSCO launched live trade receivables on blockchain, Zcash sealed a $1.7 billion pool after a four-year vulnerability, and Storj entered bankruptcy. Watch for the FOMC rate decision Wednesday at 2:00 p.m. Eastern, the Senate's August 8 Clarity Act recess deadline, and whether Bitcoin ETF outflows accelerate or stabilize into next week.
body: Bitcoin ETFs have recorded three consecutive weeks of inflows, marking the first such streak since early May, but the weekly total conceals sharp late-week turbulence that raises questions about the durability of the rebound. Per CoinDesk's reporting, U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs took in $33.79 million for the week ended July 24, though the products shed $465.26 million on Thursday and Friday alone, with BlackRock's IBIT product accounting for nearly $415 million of those late-week outflows. The desk's ETF flows board confirms the pattern: bitcoin ETFs posted a net outflow of $11.6 million on July 27, after three consecutive weeks of net inflows, signaling that institutional demand remains conditional.

The broader market posture reflects caution. Per the desk's Market Pulse board, the Fear and Greed index stands at 29, a reading of Fear, and bitcoin trades at $63,858.98, down 48.8 percent from its 12-month high. The desk's Whale Watch board shows bitcoin flowing onto exchanges over the past 24 hours, with $119 million inflows to OKX against $115 million outflows from Kraken, a net movement onto exchanges that typically precedes selling pressure. Across major assets, the desk's boards show no sustained conviction: Ethereum trades above its 24-hour entry but remains 60.2 percent below its 12-month peak, and Solana has fallen 70.1 percent from its yearly high. Leverage metrics on OKX show bitcoin longs outnumbering shorts by 1.85 to 1, but funding rates have compressed to 7.1 percent annualized, suggesting reduced appetite for leveraged exposure.

Regulatorymomentum, by contrast, accelerated sharply. BlackRock, Fidelity, Franklin Templeton, Goldman Sachs, and SoFi have publicly endorsed the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act in recent days, as the desk reported, applying pressure before the Senate begins its August 8 recess. Yet the endorsements mask a significant institutional divide: JPMorgan opposes stablecoin yield provisions that Coinbase and the crypto industry view as essential. The desk's reporting also shows that on the same day institutional finance lined up behind the bill, Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission filed a criminal complaint against Bitkub exchange and two former directors for concealing a $50 million cyberattack in 2021 and making false statements in regulatory filings, establishing precedent for how emerging-market regulators enforce disclosure obligations beyond U.S. jurisdiction.

Elsewhere, operational and structural shifts were significant. Lido deployed its largest upgrade since 2023, consolidating $16.5 billion in staked ether onto Ethereum's post-Pectra validator design while requiring its 34 professional node operators to post locked ETH bonds for the first time, reducing total validator count by roughly one-third and cutting network attestation messages by approximately 29 percent per epoch. Circle acquired nearly 1,000 blockchain-anchored patents from IBM, making it the largest blockchain patent holder in the United States, though the reporting does not disclose strategic intent. Core Scientific signed a 15-year, 529 megawatt lease with AMD for AI data center capacity worth potentially $14 billion in base contracted revenue, while terminating its Block ASIC chip agreement and recording a $41.9 million charge. POSCO International began tokenizing actual trade receivables on the Injective blockchain in a pilot with LG CNS, embedding compliance rules into digitized assets to accelerate settlement. Zcash activated its Ironwood upgrade, sealing its Orchard shielded pool containing $1.7 billion after researchers discovered a counterfeiting bug that went undetected for four years. A federal judge blocked Minnesota's prediction market ban as likely preempted by the Commodity Exchange Act, establishing that the CFTC holds jurisdiction over prediction market contracts as swaps. Russia's central bank published draft regulations establishing tiered capital requirements ranging from $570,000 to $2.8 million for digital asset platforms ahead of a full crypto framework launching in September.

Storj Labs filed for voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy while pledging to continue network operations and proposing a mechanism for token holders to convert holdings to equity, contingent on court approval and subject to bankruptcy law's priority hierarchy. Separately, the New York Times reported that Binance adopted a policy in April 2025 routing most foreign law enforcement data requests through the United Arab Emirates government and Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties, substantially increasing response times and forcing international investigators to prepare for less direct exchange access.

corrected: The Bottom Line described whale flows as moving onto exchanges without naming the window. That was the 24-hour picture at the time of publication; over the two days the Whale Watch board covers, the net ran the other way, off exchanges. The claim now states the window it describes. Nothing else in this edition changed.
